```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(effsize)
library(gt)

dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Regenerate the synthetic data if it isn't there yet, so this report is
# reproducible from a clean checkout with a single `quarto render`.
if (!file.exists("data/participants.csv")) {
  source("R/00_generate_data.R")
}
```

> **Data provenance & ethics.** All data in this report are **synthetic**, generated
> by `R/00_generate_data.R`. There are no human subjects, no protected health
> information, and no real clinical records. The workflow is written to mirror an
> IRB-approved, de-identified pipeline: participants are referenced only by an
> arbitrary study ID (`ENL-001`, …), and no identifying fields exist in the data.

## Background

The Emotion and Neurodiversity Laboratory studies the social and emotional
experiences of neurodivergent youth. A current line of work asks whether **facial
expressions and other non-verbal behaviors predict conversational success and
satisfaction**, and whether those relationships differ between autistic and
non-autistic adolescents.

This report demonstrates the full data-processing chain for a study of that shape:
raw behavioral coding + questionnaire responses → cleaning and scoring → statistical
analysis → a poster-ready figure.

**Research questions**

1. Do autistic and non-autistic participants differ in facial-expression behavior
   (smiling) and in self-reported conversation satisfaction?
2. Do facial expressions and smile reciprocity predict conversational success, and
   is that relationship moderated by group?

---

## 1. Load and inspect the raw data

```{r load}
participants <- read_csv("data/participants.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
csq_raw      <- read_csv("data/csq_items.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(participants)
```

The questionnaire arrives "raw": wide, un-scored, with two reverse-coded items
(`csq_3`, `csq_7`) and some missing responses.

```{r peek-csq}
head(csq_raw)
```

---

## 2. Clean and score the questionnaire

This is the core data-processing task: reverse-score the negatively-worded items,
handle missing responses with a pro-rated mean, and compute a total
Conversation Satisfaction score.

```{r score}
reverse_items <- c("csq_3", "csq_7")
item_cols     <- paste0("csq_", 1:8)

csq_scored <- csq_raw %>%
  # 1. Reverse-code the negatively-worded items (Likert 1-5 -> 6 - x)
  mutate(across(all_of(reverse_items), ~ 6 - .x)) %>%
  # 2. Count how many of the 8 items each person answered
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    n_answered = sum(!is.na(c_across(all_of(item_cols)))),
    # 3. Pro-rated total: mean of answered items x 8, but only if >= 6 answered
    csq_total = if_else(
      n_answered >= 6,
      round(mean(c_across(all_of(item_cols)), na.rm = TRUE) * 8, 1),
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(participant_id, n_answered, csq_total)

# Simple internal-consistency check (Cronbach-style) on the scored items
alpha_data <- csq_raw %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(reverse_items), ~ 6 - .x)) %>%
  select(all_of(item_cols))
k <- ncol(alpha_data)
item_vars <- apply(alpha_data, 2, var, na.rm = TRUE)
total_var <- var(rowSums(alpha_data, na.rm = TRUE))
cronbach_alpha <- (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(item_vars) / total_var)

cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha (8 CSQ items): %.2f\n", cronbach_alpha))
```

Merge the scored questionnaire back onto the participant-level behavioral data:

```{r merge}
dat <- participants %>%
  left_join(csq_scored, by = "participant_id") %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("non-autistic", "autistic")))

# Export a clean analysis-ready file (and an Excel-friendly copy)
write_csv(dat, "outputs/analysis_ready.csv")
glimpse(dat)
```

## 3. Descriptives by group

```{r descriptives}
dat %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    `Smiling (AU12), M` = mean(au12_lip_corner_puller),
    `Smile reciprocity, M` = mean(smile_reciprocity),
    `CSQ total, M` = mean(csq_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Conversational success, M` = mean(conversational_success),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Table 1. Descriptive statistics by group") %>%
  gtsave("outputs/table1_descriptives.html")
```

```{r descriptives-show}
#| echo: false
dat %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    `Smiling (AU12)` = round(mean(au12_lip_corner_puller), 2),
    `Smile reciprocity` = round(mean(smile_reciprocity), 2),
    `CSQ total` = round(mean(csq_total, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Conv. success` = round(mean(conversational_success), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## 4. Group comparisons

Do the groups differ in smiling and in conversation satisfaction? We report Welch's
*t*-tests with **Cohen's *d*** effect sizes (effect size, not just *p*).

```{r ttests}
compare_group <- function(var, label) {
  f <- reformulate("group", response = var)
  tt <- t.test(f, data = dat)
  d  <- effsize::cohen.d(dat[[var]], dat$group, na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(
    Outcome = label,
    `M (non-autistic)` = round(tt$estimate[1], 2),
    `M (autistic)`     = round(tt$estimate[2], 2),
    t  = round(tt$statistic, 2),
    df = round(tt$parameter, 1),
    p  = signif(tt$p.value, 3),
    `Cohen's d` = round(d$estimate, 2)
  )
}

bind_rows(
  compare_group("au12_lip_corner_puller", "Smiling (AU12)"),
  compare_group("conversational_success", "Conversational success"),
  compare_group("csq_total",              "CSQ total")
)
```

---

## 5. Does non-verbal behavior predict conversational success?

A linear model predicting conversational success from smiling and smile
reciprocity, with a **group interaction** to test whether the payoff of smiling
differs by group.

```{r regression}
m <- lm(
  conversational_success ~ scale(au12_lip_corner_puller) * group +
    scale(smile_reciprocity) + scale(au04_brow_lowerer),
  data = dat
)

tidy(m) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  rename(term = term, estimate = estimate, SE = std.error,
         t = statistic, p = p.value)

cat(sprintf("\nModel R-squared: %.2f (adj. %.2f)\n",
            summary(m)$r.squared, summary(m)$adj.r.squared))
```

**Reading the model.** Smiling and smile reciprocity are positive predictors of
conversational success; the `scale(au12...):groupautistic` term is the interaction —
a negative value means smiling is associated with a somewhat smaller gain in
conversational success in the autistic group (a controlled, synthetic effect built
into the data generator, recovered here by the analysis).

## 6. Poster-ready figure

```{r figure}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
theme_poster <- theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey35"),
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

group_cols <- c("non-autistic" = "#2C7FB8", "autistic" = "#D95F0E")

p <- ggplot(dat, aes(au12_lip_corner_puller, conversational_success, color = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Smiling predicts conversational success",
    subtitle = "Association is present in both groups, with a steeper slope for non-autistic adolescents (synthetic data)",
    x = "Smiling intensity (facial action unit AU12, mean)",
    y = "Conversational success (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_poster

p
ggsave("outputs/figure_conversational_success.png", p,
       width = 8.5, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
```

The figure is saved at 300 dpi to `outputs/figure_conversational_success.png`,
ready to drop into a conference poster.

## 7. Mini literature review

A brief review situating this analysis within the ENL / Center for Autism Research
line of work on facial affect and social-emotional processing in autism.

- **Zampella, C. J., Bennetto, L., & Herrington, J. D. (2020).** Computer vision
  analysis of reduced interpersonal affect coordination in youth with autism
  spectrum disorder. *Autism Research, 13*(12), 2133–2142.
  <https://doi.org/10.1002/aur.2334>
  — The direct precedent for this design: automated facial coding shows that
  *interpersonal affect coordination* (aligning the form and timing of facial
  affect with a partner) is reduced in autistic youth. Motivates using smiling and
  **smile reciprocity** as predictors of conversational success.

- **Herrington, J. D., et al. (2016).** Anxiety and social deficits have distinct
  relationships with amygdala function in autism spectrum disorder. *Social
  Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 11*(6), 907–914.
  <https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/scw015>
  — Establishes that social and emotional processes in autism are separable rather
  than unitary, supporting analyses that model group differences rather than
  assuming a single "autism effect."

- **Mazefsky, C. A., Herrington, J., et al. (2013).** The role of emotion
  regulation in autism spectrum disorder. *Journal of the American Academy of Child
  & Adolescent Psychiatry, 52*(7), 679–688.
  <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaac.2013.05.006>
  — Frames why the emotional/affective side of social interaction is central to
  outcomes for autistic youth, motivating the satisfaction construct measured here.

- **Baltrušaitis, T., Zadeh, A., Lim, Y. C., & Morency, L.-P. (2018).** OpenFace
  2.0: Facial behavior analysis toolkit. *IEEE FG 2018.*
  — Methods reference for the automated facial action-unit extraction (AU06, AU12,
  AU04) that the synthetic variables in this demo emulate.

> These citations were verified against public sources for this demo. For a live
> submission, confirm each against the lab's current reference manager and add any
> in-press work.
